item: The lxml extraction is bracketed in RC2's native in-flight black box, inside the extraction lock
summary: extract_article wraps the locked extraction in native_call('lxml') (src/monitoring/native_inflight.py, a 128-byte memory-mapped counter file the next boot reads), directly inside _LXML_LOCK and around the whole _extract_locked call: the lock covers the parse, the walk and the release of the trees, and the faulting frame of the 2026-10-14 SIGABRT could be any of them. It sits after the live gauge's holding mark and before its released mark, on a return and on a raise, so those two stay the first statement of the hold and of its finally (the existing AST pin and a new ordering test). A worker waiting for the lock is not counted as in lxml, a raise leaves nothing in flight and still raises, an empty page never reaches the bracket. Counts only; the module never raises and never swallows the body's exception. Cost, measured alone (python -I, three runs, medians of 15 timed blocks of 20,000 calls): entering and leaving the bracket takes 3.38 to 3.53 microseconds against 0.34 to 0.36 for an empty context manager in the same loop, so about 3.0 to 3.2 microseconds per extraction, INSIDE the hold (two stores into the mapped file under the module's lock). Against the 4.3 to 4.8 ms of an 8 KB extraction and the 28 to 30 ms of a 64 KB one (micro_marks.py, on the gauge PR's head) that is about 0.07 and 0.01 percent; no pass-level run was made, the gauge's own A/B could not resolve a microsecond. Proof: 6 tests (the slot counts one call in flight while the body runs and remembers the entry; a raising extraction leaves nothing in flight and the lock is given up; the bracket opens and closes with the lock held; the bracket sits between the gauge's holding and released marks on a return and on a raise; a worker waiting for the lock is not counted; an empty page never reaches the bracket); 4 mutants (bracket opened before holding, bracket not called, bracket outside the lock, bracket closed after released), all killed.
